title: The Brain Paradox: Four Extra Listeners Cut Rescue to 31%
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — John Darley & Bibb Latané (1968): NYU Intercom Emergency & Diffusion of Responsibility, grounded in John M. Darley, Bibb Latane (1968) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that sparked by public debate after the 1964 Queens attack on Kitty Genovese, John Darley and Bibb Latané tested in 1968 whether larger groups actually slow down emergency help rather than guaranteeing safety in numbers.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: At NYU, each student sat alone in a small cubicle wearing headphones with an intercom microphone, told that microphones rotated automatically every two minutes to protect privacy.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- John M. Darley, Bibb Latane (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025589
- Peter Fischer, Joachim I. Krueger, Tobias Greitemeyer, Claudia Vogrincic et al. (2011). The bystander-effect: A meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023304
- Janet T. Spence, John M. Darley, Donald J. Foss (1999). Preface by Janet T. Spence, John M. Darley, and Donald J. Foss. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ps.50.010199.100001
